title: Mordanting cotton and linen with rhubarb leaves
subtitle: Using rhubarb leaf liquor as a tannin mordant for plant-fibre dyeing
excerpt: Rhubarb leaves are rich in oxalic acid and tannins that help plant dyes bond to cotton and linen. A rhubarb leaf mordant bath is the simplest home method for preparing plant fibres to accept natural dye without synthetic mordants. The leaves themselves give a pale yellow-green as a bonus.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from traditional natural dyeing practice. The use of rhubarb leaf liquor as a preliminary mordant for plant fibres is documented in modern natural dye literature and traces back to traditional Central Asian dyeing practice. The oxalic acid content of rhubarb leaves is the active agent.

glossaryTerms.definition: A plant-derived tannin used to pre-treat cotton and linen before dyeing. Tannins provide surface attachment sites for dye molecules on fibres that lack the protein surface that metallic mordants bind to on wool.
A substance that helps dye bond permanently to fibre. Metallic mordants (alum, iron, copper) are standard for wool; tannin mordants are used for cotton and linen.

content.text: for cotton and linen because the leaf liquor contains oxalic acid and polyphenols that bond lightly to plant fibre. This light bonding gives subsequent

molecules and dye molecules more to hold onto. The rhubarb leaf bath is spring-gathered from the leaves that are normally discarded when harvesting rhubarb stems for eating. Do not eat rhubarb leaves: they are toxic if ingested.

attrs.title: Rhubarb leaf safety
attrs.body: Rhubarb leaves are toxic if eaten. Wear gloves and apron. Work outdoors or ventilated. Leaf bath via foul drain.

attrs.title: Dye-plant cross-reference
attrs.body: Rhubarb (Rheum x hybridum) is a common kitchen garden perennial. See the Garden tutorial on growing rhubarb for cultivation guidance.

items.name: Fresh rhubarb leaves
items.qty: equal weight to or slightly more than the fibre being mordanted

items.name: Cotton or linen yarn or fabric, pre-wetted

content.text: Chop the rhubarb leaves and simmer in water at 80°C for 45 to 60 minutes until the liquid is a dark yellow-green. Strain out the plant material. The resulting liquor is the mordant bath. Use it warm, not hot; allow it to cool to 50 to 60°C before entering the fibre.

Enter the pre-wetted cotton or linen into the cooled rhubarb leaf bath. Hold at 50 to 60°C for 60 minutes, turning regularly. Do not boil the fibre in the leaf bath: high temperatures can weaken cotton and linen fibres and degrade the polyphenols in the mordant. After 60 minutes, remove the fibre, wring gently, and either proceed immediately to the dye-bath or rinse lightly first.

The rhubarb mordant bath gives a pale yellow-green colour to the fibre even before dyeing; this is normal and comes from the leaf compounds. Once dyed, the fibre will take colour more deeply than undyed cotton or linen. For best results, follow the rhubarb mordant with a second alum acetate bath (15% weight-of-fibre) to improve bonding before the dye-bath.

items.problem: The mordanted cotton or linen still takes dye very poorly
items.cause: The rhubarb leaf mordant alone is not sufficient for deep colour; it is a weak mordant compared with metallic alum acetate for plant fibres
items.fix: Follow the rhubarb leaf bath with an alum acetate mordant bath (15% weight-of-fibre) for stronger colour uptake. The rhubarb leaf bath improves the result but is not a complete replacement for alum acetate on cotton or linen.

items.problem: The dye colour changed noticeably during the mordant step
items.cause: The oxalic acid in the rhubarb leaf bath reacted with a metallic residue in the pot or an existing dye on the fibre
items.fix: Use a clean, dedicated pot that has not been used with iron or copper mordants recently. Oxalic acid and iron react to produce a strong greying effect on subsequent colours.
